character_and_relationship_context: Aminata Diallo is a young woman who lives in a rented room in a bustling district of Bamako. She works as the only woman on a construction crew, where she is known for recalculating load-bearing estimates in her head. Her mother died when she was twelve, and she has since developed a habit of counting everything: bricks, costs, weeks until her accounting exam. She keeps a notebook of figures and dates, and hides an emergency fund under a floorboard. At night she studies by lamp for an accounting course at a community center. She is saving for a proper room where her sister can live with her and attend school, but does not speak of this aloud. She holds her trowel every day and checks measurements twice. She knows the young man at the tea stall only by sight from the exam prep class; they have smiled at each other but never spoken, and she has no other connection to him. She has never accepted a gift or favor from a man she does not know well. Once, when offered a free drink by a stall owner, she politely declined and bought her own. She habitually avoids stopping on her walk home because delays mean arriving after dark.
objective_situation: It is nearly dusk, and Aminata is walking back from the community center after her accounting exam prep. She passes a small tea stall where a young man she has seen at the center several times—he often smiles at her—raises his hand. He offers to buy her a glass of sweet tea; the stall is warm and lit, and he seems to mean no harm. She is tired, her soles ache, and she still has a long walk ahead to her room. The man is waiting for her answer as a vendor pours another glass.
state_and_available_memories: Her legs ache from hauling cement and the walk to the center. She is thirsty and has not eaten since early afternoon. Her mind is still heavy with the accounting problems from the prep session. The warm lamp in the stall reminds her of studying by her own kerosene lamp late at night. The man’s smile brings back the memory of a boy at the market who smiled before asking her to carry his goods for free. The scent of sweet tea reminds her of the glass her mother bought her on market days before she died.
name: Aminata Diallo
